Man Buys New 2017 Dodge Viper GTC for $127,885, Drives 854 Miles, Sells for $242,500

Photo: Bring a Trailer
Remember when you could buy a brand-new Dodge Viper in the high five-figure range? Later on it was low six-figures, but regardless, those days are long gone. And if you want a pristine fifth-generation example with a top spec, you'll find yourself spending 2026 Corvette ZR1 money.
Case in point, this 2017 Viper GTC TA 1.0, which just sold for a whopping $242,500 at auction. The seller had previously purchased the car new for $127,885. Not a bad haul for a supercar the likes of which has since gone extinct. The odometer currently shows just 854 miles, which is next to nothing. I'm not sure I'd want to add to it, though. This might be more of a collectible than anything else.
Let's not forget how the fifth-gen Viper was already an endangered species back in 2017. Dodge discontinued production that very same year, so these cars were always going to be collectibles.
Personally, I always thought the final-gen Viper was one of the best-looking American sports cars/supercars ever made. Everything from the proportions to the stance... it's absolutely stunning. Not as stunning as the first-gen model, but stunning nonetheless.
I still can't get over the fact that we live in a world without a modern-day Dodge Viper. Stellantis could definitely use a "win" after this whole Charger Daytona fiasco, and a new-gen Viper would silence a lot of critics - as long as they don't mess it up.
Speaking of not messing things up, this spec right here . Just wow.
The Venom Black exterior with the black Sidewinder II wheels, plus the optional Time Attack 1.0 Package, which makes the car a lot more interesting from a driving enthusiast's standpoint - you've got the revised two-mode Bilstein DampTronic system courtesy of the TA suspension, while other visual and practical highlights include the GTS hood, rear spoiler, tinted windows, HID headlights, side-exit exhaust outlets, Brembo brakes, and Pirelli P Zero Corsa rubber.
The cockpit is as driver-focused as they get, with those power-adjustable Sabelt seats, power-adjustable pedals, carbon fiber accents, Alcantara headliner, an 18-speaker Harman Kardon high-performance sound system, a backup camera, and more. There's a lot of Laguna premium leather here, including on the door panels, instrument panel and even the center console - thanks to the optional Laguna Interior Package.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Last but not least, we've got the Viper's greatest asset , it's magnificent naturally aspirated 8.4-liter V10 engine, good for 640 horsepower and 600 lb-ft of torque. Everything gets sent to the rear wheels via a Tremec six-speed manual transmission and a limited slip differential.
It goes without saying that should the Viper get revived any time soon, there's no way it'll be putting down less than 900 horsepower. And no, I'm not just guessing, because for most of its history, the Dodge Viper was way more powerful than the standard Corvette, and just as powerful as any of the flagship Vette specs.
This fifth-gen Viper GTC packs a similar punch to a C7 Corvette Z06, while older versions were somewhere in the same ballpark as the C6 ZR1. So it stands to reason that a next-gen Viper would try to match the C8 Corvette at the top end of the range. Meaning either the ZR1 or the ZR1X.

Tesla has parked a fleet of mobile Supercharger stalls at some of its busiest stations in California and Arizona to handle the Thanksgiving travel crush. The company says 29 temporary stalls are live, on top of 1,027 permanent stalls it opened in the US over the last 56 days.
It’s the most organized holiday push we’ve seen from Tesla’s charging team. And it comes with on-site attendants to manage lines and a virtual waitlist now running at 300 sites.
Where Tesla parked the mobile Superchargers
Tesla’s charging account shared a single composite photo showing four locations. The stall counts in it add up to exactly 29:
Firebaugh, CA: +10 stalls
Bakersfield, CA (Olive Dr): +8 stalls
Bakersfield, CA (Copus Rd): +4 stalls
Holbrook, AZ: +7 stalls
Firebaugh, CA: two trailers add 10 stalls (Image: Tesla Charging)
Firebaugh gets the biggest boost: two flatbed trailers loaded with Supercharger posts and tall power cabinets, parked right under the station’s solar canopy.

Bakersfield, CA, Olive Dr: +8 stalls (Image: Tesla Charging)
Three of the four sites are in California’s Central Valley, the stretch between Los Angeles and the Bay Area where Thanksgiving Supercharger lines have been a problem for years. Bakersfield’s Copus Rd station was already on the list of sites where Tesla offered free off-peak Supercharging in 2021 to spread out holiday demand. So Tesla knows exactly where the pain is.
Bakersfield, CA, Copus Rd: +4 stalls (Image: Tesla Charging)
Holbrook is the outlier. It’s a small town on I-40 in northern Arizona, the main corridor between Southern California and Albuquerque, where there aren’t many alternatives if a station is full.
Holbrook, AZ: +7 stalls (Image: Tesla Charging)
The Copus Rd and Holbrook units sit directly on the pavement rather than on trailers. Tesla didn’t say whether any of these mobile stalls run off the grid or off onboard batteries, like the Megapack Chargers it deployed for the holidays in 2024 . Those battery trailers haven’t been flawless, either: one burned at the Baker, CA Supercharger on New Year’s Day 2023.
The bigger number is the 1,027 permanent stalls
Twenty-nine mobile stalls is a rounding error. The real holiday prep is the permanent build.
Tesla says it opened 1,027 stalls across 91 US sites in the last 56 days. That’s about 18 stalls a day, and an average of more than 11 stalls per new site.
For comparison, Paren’s data showed Tesla added 1,287 US fast-charging ports in Q3 , or roughly 14 per day. The methodologies aren’t identical, but it points to Tesla speeding up deployment by about 30% ahead of the holidays. In that same quarter, IONNA added 378 ports and Walmart added 344.
Tesla also says it has boosted uptime and service dispatch for the travel window, and it’s putting attendants at its busiest sites to manage queues.
Then there’s the waitlist. Tesla launched its virtual queue pilot at just five Supercharger sites in May , a full year after it promised the feature following a fight between owners at a full station. It’s now live at 300 sites.
For context, Tesla said its US network handled more than 2 million sessions and delivered over 70 GWh between the Wednesday and Sunday of Thanksgiving 2025, with only 0.76% of sessions involving a wait.
Electrek’s Take
We’ve been covering Tesla’s Thanksgiving stress test since 2018, when it was genuinely rough, and 2019 brought multi-hour waits in the Central Valley. This year looks like a network operator planning for a known spike instead of apologizing after it.
Twenty-nine stalls across four sites won’t make or break anyone’s weekend. But they’re going to be precisely the stations that get hammered every year.
The 18 stalls a day is what matters. We severely criticised Elon Musk after he needlessly fired Tesla’s entire charging team in 2024 as it resulted in a significant slowdown in deployment.
He stands by this criticism, but it finally looks like Tesla is getting back to its old supercharger deployment rate. Nobody else in the US is building at anything close to that pace.

By: Northern Miner Staff November 26, 2026
Cobalt prices have soared this week after the Democratic Republic of Congo announced its second export ban in less than two years, BMO Capital Markets said Thursday.
London Metal Exchange-traded cobalt futures recently hit US$43,855 (C$62,360) a tonne, up from US$33,080 on Monday, BMO commodity analysts Helen Amos and George Heppel said Thursday in a note. The ban takes effect Nov. 30 and includes previously authorized shipments that have not left the country by then, according to Congo’s strategic minerals regulator, ARECOMS.
“Authorities plan to review the ban after four months, while also reassessing the existing quota allocation system,” Amos and Heppel said. The review does not automatically end the ban; exports can resume only after a separate regulatory decision.
Congo accounted for 230,000 of the 310,000 tonnes of cobalt mined worldwide in 2025, the United States Geological Survey estimates. Congolese miners recover much of it alongside copper. A halt to shipments can squeeze buyers overseas while cobalt continues to accumulate at home.
Immediate changes
Glencore (LSE: GLEN) has already changed how it handles cobalt under Congo’s export restrictions. The company produced 13,700 tonnes of cobalt in the first nine months of 2026, down 52% from a year earlier. It increasingly retained cobalt in solution rather than processing it into saleable hydroxide while focusing on copper production, Glencore said in October.
Chinese futures also rose after the announcement. The December cobalt contract on the Wuxi Stainless Steel Exchange hit their daily limit of 316 yuan per kilogram on Tuesday, the highest since Aug. 18, Reuters reported.
Congo’s first export ban ran from February to October 2025, when the regulator introduced quotas. Miners have no automatic right to carry unused quotas forward, the regulator said in its Nov. 23 notice.

Aerial view of the Don Mario operation in Bolivia. Credit: Orvana Minerals.
By: Northern Miner Staff November 26, 2026
Orvana Minerals (TSX: ORV; US-OTC: ORVMF) faces a bondholders’ meeting Monday after its Bolivian unit breached financial conditions on about $25 million (C$35.5 million) in bonds issued to expand its Don Mario gold and copper plant. The stock dropped.
Empresa Minera Paitití has until Dec. 8 to restore compliance unless bondholders extend the deadline, waive the requirements or amend them. The remaining bonds mature Feb. 19, according to Orvana’s annual results released after markets closed Wednesday.
Orvana shares dropped 3% to C$1.29 Thursday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$176 million ($124 million). The stock has traded between C$1.09 and C$2.93 in the past year.
“We remain focused on progressively reducing the debt incurred to fund the investment in the Don Mario plant expansion, in accordance with the agreed terms,” CEO Juan Gavidia said in a Nov. 9 update.
Higher throughput
Don Mario, located about 380 km east of Santa Cruz de la Sierra, is processing 1,300 tonnes of stockpiled oxide ore a day. Orvana aims to reach its design capacity of 1,700 tonnes a day by the end of December, weeks before the bonds mature.
Orvana expects the plant to produce 22,000 to 26,000 oz. of gold and 14 million to 16 million lb. of copper in fiscal 2027.
Don Mario produced 1,597 oz. of gold and 411,274 lb. of copper in the year ended Sept. 30, including output from commissioning tests and the initial ramp-up.
Covenant breach
The Bolivian unit breached financial covenants as of both June 30 and Sept. 30. Orvana cited the accounting impact of Bolivia’s new official exchange-rate regime and road blockades in May and June that delayed work at Don Mario. The subsidiary fully repaid its first bond program on Nov. 7.
Orvana’s liquidity forecasts assume lenders will not demand early repayment because of the covenant breaches. The company is supporting its Bolivian subsidiary through intercompany funding while Don Mario ramps up. A separate $25-million prepayment facility falls due in three instalments between April and June 2027.
The company expects to cover $111.7 million in commitments due within a year through its $42-million cash balance, forecast operating cash flow, renewed revolving credit lines and VAT refunds. Orvana’s so-called Bonds II carry a fixed annual interest rate of 10%, and the final quarterly covenant test before their February maturity falls on Dec. 31.
Stronger year
The bond talks follow a stronger financial year. Orvana swung to fiscal 2026 net income of about $36 million, compared with a year-earlier loss of $12.3 million, as revenue soared 84% to $182 million and operating cash flow more than tripled to $57.1 million. At the group level, Orvana ended September with $42 million in cash and $120.3 million in current liabilities.
At Orovalle in northern Spain, gold production rose 29% to 37,775 oz. in fiscal 2026, above its guidance range of 34,000 to 37,000 ounces. Orvana expects 27,000 to 31,000 oz. this fiscal year as crews develop deeper levels at Carlés and less skarn ore is available at Boinás.
In Argentina, Orvana plans about 19,500 metres of drilling at its Taguas project between December 2026 and May 2027, with a preliminary budget of $15 million. The program combines drilling to improve confidence in the near-surface gold-silver resource with deeper exploration for a possible copper-gold system, subject to suitable weather and site conditions.
Further exploration at Taguas will depend on available funding as Orvana manages debt repayments and completes Don Mario’s ramp-up, Orvana said.

Currawong Family Is a Tiny Home With Three Bedrooms, Full-Size Appliances, and Ample Storage
11 photos
Photo: Unplgd Tiny Homes
Tiny homes may be compact living solutions, but that doesn’t mean they are only intended for singles or couples. Though downsizing can present challenges, especially when it comes to families, there are now countless modern designs that make room for a comfortable family life. The Currawong Family from Unplgd Tiny Homes is one such example.
The Currawong Family is a well-designed tiny home on wheels that proves a smaller footprint can still accommodate the needs of a family. With three separate sleeping spaces, including a downstairs bedroom and two lofts, it represents a practical solution for larger households looking to live comfortably in a smaller footprint.
Part of Unplgd Tiny Homes’ Currawong range, along with the single-level Currawong Chick and the two-bedroom Currawong Fledgling, this family-oriented tiny house is a less-expensive, non-customizable offer compared to the Australian builder’s standard range. It’s also narrower at 2.5 meters (8.2 feet) wide (the other models offered by Unplgd are 3 meters/9.8 feet wide), but this means they are easier to transport, relocate, and fit down regular driveways.
This model is built on a triple-axle custom trailer and measures 9 meters (29.5 feet) long and 4.5 meters (14.7 feet) high. It’s a modern, eye-catching compact dwelling that can sleep six or more people thanks to a clever layout and space optimization, but more importantly, it is versatile and can adapt to many lifestyles.
Photo: Unplgd Tiny Homes On the outside, it displays a contemporary, two-tone design with a combination of dark charcoal corrugated metal panels and gray fiber-cement sheeting with fireproof paint. The interior is characterized by simplicity and practicality, but it feels inviting and contemporary with its white walls, custom cabinetry, vinyl flooring, and modern furnishings.
Aimed at growing families who need more bedroom space and a bit more privacy without giving up the practical tiny home lifestyle, it features three bedrooms, giving everyone their own intimate space, plus a welcoming living area for evening gatherings, a full kitchen, a dedicated dining area, and a generous bathroom with laundry facilities. All these are included in a narrow design, but the interior doesn’t feel cramped and offers the functionality needed for day-to-day routines.
Taking advantage of the home’s generous height, the builder created two comfortable loft bedrooms with queen-size beds and standing-height bedside landing. Accessed via a ladder or a staircase, the lofts also integrate storage solutions, are very luminous, and come with privacy walls. One of the lofts even includes a full wall of cabinetry, providing plenty of storage for clothes and other belongings.
Photo: Unplgd Tiny Homes The third bedroom is on the ground floor, benefits from its own glass door for direct access from the outside, and it is more accessible and convenient for everyday use. It accommodates a queen-size bed as well, and two of its walls are lined with overhead cabinets. There is also a closet for hanging clothes and some wooden ledges above the bed, perfect for books and decorations.
Beyond the comfortable sleeping arrangements, the Currawong Family has an open-plan great room downstairs, which provides enough space for family living. Located at one end of the house, the lounge can be fitted with a large sofa that folds out into a double bed when additional sleeping space is needed.
There is a seamless flow between the lounge and the central kitchen, making it a great area for easy cooking and entertaining. With generous countertop space, room for full-sized appliances, such as an induction cooktop, a rangehood, an oven, and a refrigerator with freezer compartment.
Photo: Unplgd Tiny Homes The all-too-familiar overhead cabinets are replaced by wooden shelves, which helps keep the space more open, but this doesn't mean there is shortage of storage in here. Apart from the lower cabinets, there is a large pantry under the loft walkway. Next to it, a built-in breakfast bar with stools adds a functional place for meals, though it wouldn’t fit the entire family.
Practicality is the best word to describe the bathroom as well. It’s a walk-through design that takes advantage of the home’s full width to integrate a large shower, a flushing toilet, a vanity, and a washing machine. A tall closet and upper cabinets above the laundry area add practical storage for linen, towels, toiletries, and cleaning products.
Photo: Unplgd Tiny Homes While the general configuration of this tiny home on wheels cannot be modified, the interior can still be customized with your choice of colors, finishes, and fittings. The home can also suit those interested in a quieter, off-grid lifestyle, with the company ready to help you equip it with the needed systems.
Founded by a couple who believe tiny living can set people free, financially and personally, Unplgd Tiny Homes introduced the Currawong range as a practical response to the ongoing housing crisis in Australia. Offering the essentials of a family home in a compact design, the Currawong Family tiny house is indeed a practical solution for households looking to reduce their footprint and cut living costs. Pricing for this model starts at AUD$195,000, which is about USD$129,280 at current exchange rates.

The Flashiest Camper Around Is Now Even Better: See the 2027 Keystone Reign 15RB
24 photos
Photo: Keystone RV
Who doesn't like their adventure trailer with a bit more oomph? That was not the reasoning behind the creation of the Reign series of adventure trailers over at Keystone RV just a couple of years ago, but it could have been. For 2027, the Reign 15RB is still that, but also better.
When Keystone debuted the Reign trailers , they promised they (the trailers) would solve some of the industry's biggest and most enduring problems linked to wood-reliant construction. The Reign towables would be adventure trailers, not travel trailers, that would guarantee a lifetime of enjoyment in a form factor that was still compact, lightweight, and – you guessed it – eye-catching.
They kept that promise, while also offering what was dubbed the flashiest camper around. They also did not settle for this initial win, continuing to work on the floorplans based on customer feedback. The 2027 Reign series includes five floorplans, with the 15RB coming as the second smallest of the bunch.
It's being redesigned for 2027, and the upgraded interior puts the focus back on this being a premium towable while adding extra functionality and one more sleeping berth. Seeing how this is still a compact trailer, these are no small achievements, you will agree.
Photo: Keystone RV From the outside, the Reign 15RB is the same as in previous years. That means you get a single-axle towable on a BAL huck-bolted chassis with a body of automotive aluminum painted a very special Mercedes blue that is exclusive to Keystone. Keystone calls the construction Hyper Construction, including HyperCore composite body, aluminum skin, and HyperDeck fully composite flooring.
Also unchanged are frameless tinted windows, a fully enclosed underbelly, composite entry steps, and the Edgeview exterior glow lighting system on a dimmer, which is the one that earned the trailer the moniker of being the flashiest and loudest at any campsite. The axle is a Dexter Torflex, so you get independent suspension, as well as 15-inch all-terrain tires with aluminum rims.
The original layout was a three-person one, with a front Murphy-style bed and a small booth dinette that dropped into a single bed, a galley kitchen, and a full rear bath that also gave the camper its name ("RB"). The 2027 model year brings a similar layout, but with upgrades that add extra value.
Photo: YouTube/Myles RVs The first thing that stands out is the addition of a flip-up bunk bed over the dinette, which takes the camper from a three-person to a four-person one and makes it even more appealing for families with kids. It could be that this bunk will only be available as an option, but still. It wasn't there last year.
Then, the entire cabinetry has been redesigned and now includes opening doors where you only found elastic netting before. This was a choice meant to save weight and reduce costs, but Myles from Myles RVs , who toured a 2027 unit for the first video at the bottom of the page, says that cabinetry is made of composite so that it feels sturdy, wood-like, but also light.
Keystone is also adding more storage options, particularly around the Murphy-style bed in the bedroom, which now offers overhead cubbies, matching wardrobes, and a pair of large drawers underneath. Another instance where storage is greatly improved is in the bathroom, which gets a full wall of cabinets and drawers for all your essentials – and maybe some extras as well.
Photo: YouTube/Myles RVs The most obvious result of this redesign is that the camper now looks cozier and more elegant. Introduced in 1964 as an option package on the LeMans, the Pontiac GTO is credited with having kickstarted the muscle car craze. It remained highly popular until 1971, when sales dropped to only 10,532 units. The nameplate was discontinued in 1974, with the final-year model being a package on the compact Ventura.
Pontiac sold three different generations of the GTO. The first one lasted from 1964 to 1967, with a notable redesign introduced in 1965. The second-gen model, produced from 1968 to 1972, got a significant overhaul in 1970. Finally, the third-generation GTO was produced for one single year, 1973.
The latter was also an option package for the LeMans and featured GM's Colonnade body, which eliminated the authentic hardtop design. Unlike its predecessor, it also featured prominent chrome bumpers, which were added due to then-new federal laws. The 1973 GTO was not well received by the public, with sales hitting an all-time low of 4,806 units.
The 1973 GTO is obviously the least desirable iteration of the series. Because of this, many cars are still rotting away in junkyards and barns. Pristine survivors are super rare, while restored examples are hard to come by. This silver Sport Coupe is one of those lucky examples that got a second chance and looks fresh despite being 53 years old as of 2026.
Although its design doesn't get a lot of love, I actually like the 1973 GTO. I'm a big fan of the V-shaped hood that extends into the upper side panels, the muscular rear fenders, and the flat, almost boat-tail-like rear end. The silver paint also suits this body style quite well, and the burgundy interior makes for a striking contrast.
There's no info as to when this GTO was restored, but it looks pretty much flawless inside and out. Our host doesn't open the hood but confirms that the Poncho packs a 400-cubic-inch (6.6-liter) V8 engine.
This was the standard unit in 1973. Pontiac reduced the compression ratio to 8.0:1, and oomph dropped to 230 horsepower. An optional 455-cubic-inch (7.5-liter) V8 was available with 250 horsepower. The 455 HO unit was discontinued for 1973.
While the 455 unit was exclusively paired with the automatic transmission, the 400 V8 was also offered with manual gearboxes. The three-speed unit was standard, while the four-speed was optional. This GTO was ordered with the latter.
The three-pedal layout makes this GTO pretty rare. Existing records from PHS show that only 1,113 units were equipped with the manual transmission. The figure includes 187 Coupes and 926 Sport Coupes. This GTO is a Sport Coupe. These figures are for both three- and four-speed manual cars, but the former is pretty uncommon.
The color combo could also be described as uncommon. That's mainly because the burgundy interior was only available with five exterior colors, with Ascot Silver being one of them. I'd say that fewer than 100 examples were built exactly like this. What's your take on the 1973 GTO ? Would you drive one?

BMW Australia Replacing iX Electric SUV With New iX5

Photo: BMW
The iX for Australia isn't going the way of the dodo because it sold worse than its direct rivals. BMW is pushing it out in favor of the iX5, a model donning new-gen styling and a more familiar badge. And while it may feature CLAR underpinnings, the iX5 levels up to cylindrical cells, 800 volts for ultra-fast charging, plus cell-to-pack construction, putting it closer to the Neue Klasse-based iX3 than the outgoing iX.
Given the aforementioned, keeping the iX and the incoming iX5 under the same roof makes little sense for the Australian subsidiary. Both are large zero-emission luxury SUVs, and there simply isn't enough daylight between them to justify selling both concomitantly. The iX, therefore, will be phased out locally. BMW hasn't confirmed when iX production wraps up, though.
Brendan Michel, the head of product at BMW Australia, confirmed its canning to CarExpert. Hearsay, meanwhile, suggests that iX production will be wrapped up at some point in June 2028. The iX has already been discontinued from the United States and Canadian markets. Production for these markets ended in October 2026.
Both decisions speak volumes about how the Munich-based automaker's electric vehicle strategy is changing. Compared to the iX, which rolled out in late 2020 as a standalone statement with its own styling and a unique platform that happens to be highly compatible with the Cluster Architecture, the iX5 doesn't need an entirely separate model identity from the already familiar X5.
From a commercial standpoint, BMW Australia has a compelling reason to make that switch. CarExpert highlights that only 2,424 units were shipped to Australia since its 2021 launch there, averaging in the ballpark of 500 units per annum. X5 deliveries over the same period reached just around 17,000 vehicles with gasoline, diesel, and plug-in hybrid powertrains.
Photo: BMW The redesigned X5 is coming with five confirmed powertrain flavors. The all-electric and hydrogen options bring the grand total to five, although the fuel-cell powertrain will be available in very few units and in select markets. Officially dubbed iX5 Hydrogen, that fellow is due in 2028 with confirmed exclusions that include Australia and Eastern Europe.
More than adequately powerful in 60 xDrive form, the full-electric iX5 for Australia is apparently capable of 845 kilometers (525 miles) on a full charge. By comparison, the iX in xDrive45 M Sport specification can't do better than 602 kilometers (374 miles) in one go. Naturally, the iX5 also fares better in terms of charging, with BMW claiming up to 406 instead of 175 kilowatts.
That's 2.6 times the peak rate, and yes, prospective customers need a charger that is capable of supplying that kind of power to actually experience charging at 460 kilowatts. From 10 to 80 percent state of charge, the iX5 needs only 23 minutes.
A quick search on BMW's media website also reveals that 16,789 examples of the iX were delivered globally in the first nine months of 2026, representing a 34.1 percent nosedive from the 25,463 moved a year earlier. The plug-in hybrid XM performance SUV also fell badly, with BMW reporting 4,115 versus 5,732 deliveries.

Planet One Group chairman Sanjeev Mansotra (left) shakes hands with Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye. Planet One and state miner Miferso plan to mine iron ore at Falémé and produce steel in Senegal as part of a $933-million project. Credit: Planet One Group
By: Northern Miner Staff November 26, 2026
Planet One Group and Senegalese state miner Miferso laid the foundation stone Thursday for a $933-million (C$1.33-billion) project to mine iron ore at Falémé and make steel for the country’s builders and manufacturers.
The deposits lie in the Kédougou region, about 750 km southeast of Dakar. The first stage would cost about $200 million and produce 3 million–5 million tonnes of iron ore a year, Planet One Chairman Sanjeev Mansotra told Reuters. He put peak output at 10 million tonnes a year.
“The Ministry will ensure strict compliance with the commitments made regarding local content, employment opportunities for young people in the region, transparency, and environmental protection, particularly the preservation of the Falémé River,” Mines and Geology Minister Cheikhou Oumar Seck said in Planet One’s release.
Senegal imported 722,000 tonnes of iron and steel in 2025, up 75% from a year earlier, according to the national statistics agency. The partners plan to use natural gas to turn the ore into direct-reduced iron, a feedstock for steelmaking. The government is still working to secure affordable gas for the plants, Planet One said.
High grade
Based in the United Arab Emirates, Planet One holds 80% of the venture. Miferso and the Senegalese government each hold 10%, Mansotra told Reuters. He expects debt to cover 60% of the investment and equity to cover the rest. The first stage, including mine equipment and upgrades to roads and rail, would take 12 to 18 months. Planet One expects the full project to create more than 1,200 direct and indirect jobs.
Planet One estimates the three deposits hold up to 600 million tonnes of iron ore. It gave no estimate date, resource category or overall grade. Earlier work put the iron grade at 59% in hematite at Koudékourou and an average of 43% in magnetite at Goto and Farangalia, according to a December 2025 report from Senegal’s Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative.
Infrastructure
Miferso plans a new rail line of about 310 km to connect Falémé with the national network at Tambacounda so ore can reach the coast. The state miner still listed the rail link as planned in its Nov. 9 update.
ArcelorMittal (NYSE: MT) had aimed to ship Falémé ore to its European mills. Its $2.2-billion project, agreed with Senegal in 2007, called for a new port near Dakar and first production in 2011. An arbitration tribunal ruled in 2013 that Senegal could terminate the agreements. ArcelorMittal agreed in May 2014 to pay Senegal $150 million to settle the dispute.

Mazda UK Bosses Claim the Brand Could Survive Without the MX-5 Miata
7 photos
Photo: Mazda
Mazda UK sales director Laura Brailey was asked whether the company imagines a future without the MX-5. Her answer? "Yeah, absolutely." Quite a response, particularly from a company whose little roadster has spent 37 years doing something most cars today struggle to manage. Simply put, the Miata makes the act of driving feel like the point of owning a car.
It sure doesn't sell in CX-5 numbers, and it's not as rational a car as the CX-5 either. Treating the MX-5 as just another model that happens to occupy a small corner of the sales chart, however, misses the whole reason it exists. Brailey's take should not be shouted down, though.
As of this writing, Mazda UK and every other national subsidiary isn't as dependent on the Hiroshima-built sports car for brand recognition as it was three decades ago. The CX-5 and other crossovers are the products that pay most of the bills, for assembly operations, development programs, and the next generation of cars, while the MX-5 Miata has always been a niche product.
Using this logic, it's easy to understand how the little roadster and the crossover line cater to entirely different customers. One gives the customer a sensible reason to visit a showroom. The other makes them associate the brand with the Jinba Ittai philosophy, which isn't merely a catchy phrase for brochures.
It describes the relationship between man and machine, a relationship based on responsiveness rather than burying the driving experience beneath weight, power, and electronic nannies like traction and stability control. And that's the thing.
Automakers can sell millions of practical vehicles without having a single sports car in the lineup. They cannot manufacture the same enthusiast credibility by rolling out another special edition of an SUV, though, and looking at the bigger picture, the MX-5 is arguably the purest expression of Mazda's character.
Photo: Mazda Its formula is unashamedly uncomplicated: driven wheels at the rear, engine at the front, a manual box, two seats, little in the way of comfort, and as little mass as reasonably possible. Back home in Japan, where it's called Roadster, the MX-5 Miata weighs as little as 1,010 kilograms (2,227 pounds). That configuration uses a 1.5-liter engine, which isn't available in the United States of America.
The CX-5, on the other hand, tips the scales at 1,640 kilograms (3,616 pounds) from the outset. Good for a little over 130 mechanical horsepower and 114 pound-feet (155 Newton-meters) of twist, said 1.5-liter engine of the MX-5 offers very modest figures by modern performance car standards. Thing is, the MX-5 never tried to impress on paper.
Its appeal comes exclusively from the way it drives and how that driving experience makes you feel. And with so little power on deck, it's fairly easy to feel like you're getting near the inherent limits of the car without going absurdly fast.
Back in August 2025, the Japanese automaker confirmed that over 1.25 million examples have rolled off the assembly line, maintaining the Miata's status as the Guinness World Record holder for the world's most popular two-seat sports car. The first million was reported in April 2016, after nearly 27 years of production.
Mazda UK managing director told Auto Express that the current range will continue evolving, with Brailey adding that the MX-5 will stay for as long as UK regulations permit the sale of internal combustion vehicles.
Before the Miata goes electric, the next generation will get a 2.5-liter engine from the upcoming Skyactiv-Z family. A bunch of executives have further highlighted that 1,000 kilos (2,205 pounds) is the internal target for the NE.

By: Northern Miner Staff November 26, 2026
Nearly three-quarters of respondents to a Canadian survey said local communities should have more influence over mining projects. Only 21% thought their own community had a say in those decisions.
Of the 5,074 people surveyed, 49% reported relatively high acceptance of mining and 21% expressed high trust in the industry’s ability to act responsibly. Neither measure changed significantly from 2025, community relations firm Transfert Environnement et Société and research firm Voconiq said Thursday in their second annual Social Acceptability Barometer.
“People increasingly recognize the mining sector’s economic contribution, but this does not translate into greater acceptability or trust,” study co-author Marc-Olivier Fortin, Transfert’s director of development and partnerships, said in a release. “Benefit-sharing, community influence, environmental protection and industry accountability remain central issues.”
The findings come as Ontario seeks to speed up mine approvals . The province said Tuesday it plans to scrap or streamline half the key permits and authorizations needed to advance a mine. In the survey, conducted before Ontario outlined its plans, 57% of respondents said a project should go ahead only if a majority of people in the affected community support it.
Creating jobs
People in mining regions were more open to a new mine close to home. Among those respondents, 57% said they would back a mine in their region, compared with 42% of those living outside mining regions. Across the sample, 54% said mining harms water quality.
Mining earned its highest economic marks for creating jobs, with an average score of 4.16 out of five, up from 4.10 last year. The biggest gain among the four economic measures was in mining’s perceived importance to quality of life, up to 3.80 from 3.67. Scores for how fairly mining’s benefits are shared stayed below the midpoint of the scale.
Among First Nations respondents, 85% said Indigenous Peoples should own a stake in projects on their traditional lands. First Nations respondents rated the fairness of benefit-sharing at 2.91 out of five, compared with 2.63 among Métis respondents. Too few Inuit respondents took part for a separate analysis, the researchers said.
The survey ran from July 30 to Sept. 1 through the Léger Opinion online panel. The researchers used age and gender quotas and didn’t weight the results to match Canada’s population.

5 German Legends That Ruled the Autobahn in the 1990s
31 photos
Photo: Brabus
There was a time, not long ago, when the fastest way to cross Germany without being a passenger in a jet plane was to drive a large German sedan or coupe with a big engine, a full tank of gas, and a mostly empty left lane ahead of you.
That time was during the 1990s, and that empty left lane was obviously found on one of the thousand of miles of Autobahn, many of which were still without a speed limit back then. As most of you know, Germany’s highway network has pretty much always had a special place in car culture, and the reason for that is because much of it had no general speed limit.
Even though since 1978 there has been an advised speed limit of 130 kph (81 mph), which has meanwhile become enforced in many areas, on a lot of unrestricted stretches of the Autobahn it has remained just an advice.
For most German carmakers, especially the premium ones from Munich, Stuttgart, and Ingolstadt, this transformed the Autobahn into something that no other country could offer. It was simply a public road playground where a car’s top speed was just a practical consideration instead of a number in a brochure or a reason to lose your license.
In fact, it was all fun and games until 1987, when BMW electronically restricted the V12-powered 750i to 250 kph (155 mph), indirectly triggering a Gentleman’s Agreement that aligned all the other premium carmakers, with the exception of Porsche, in a similar situation. Until well into the 2000s, every fast Audi, BMW and Mercedes-Benz has had a 250 kph (155 mph) speed limit from the factory.
That limit was chosen for safety reasons, not for a lack of performance, though. It was originally meant to stop a horsepower race from getting out of hand, and, for the most part, it worked. On the other hand, that agreement also helped create and cultivate the development of a peculiar kind of car. These cars had far more power than they needed to reach their limited top speeds, with much better brakes, steering and suspension than most other rivals.
Their owners knew exactly how much faster these cars could go if someone tampered with their limiters. On top of it, some carmakers and especially tuners completely ignored that agreement, and the cars that broke it became legends in the process.
As it turns out, what made these vehicles special wasn’t only their speed, but also the way they delivered it and especially sustained it. The true Autobahn monsters that resulted from this were not lightweight sports cars or screaming exotics, but executive sedans, grand tourers and even station wagons that looked almost ordinary, but were drenched in soft leather, had high tech climate control systems and a comfortable suspension setup.
They all could comfortably sustain a high speed that would have made most regular drivers, even today, a bit nervous. With that in mind, I decided to compile a short list of the coolest Autobahn warriors of the 1990s, which is seen by many as the beginning of the golden era of public German speed.
Alpina B10 Bi-Turbo: The First Executive Sedan to Ignore the Gentleman’s Agreement in the 1990s As mentioned before, the German car industry, save for Porsche, had just agreed to limit its cars to 250 kph (155 mph) in the second half of the 1980s. Among the entities that had no use for such a silly agreement were boutique carmakers and established tuners, with a small company in Bavaria being one of them.
Alpina, which is now wholly owned by BMW, first responded to such nonsense by building a four-door executive sedan that could top 290 kph (180 mph), called the B10 Bi-Turbo. Not just a BMW tuner but a licensed manufacturer at the time, Alpina had spent the previous two decades turning Bimmers into faster, more refined versions.
Photo: Alpina Its new flagship was shown at the 1989 Geneva Motor Show, and was based on the otherwise inconspicuous BMW 535i (E34). The engineers in Buchloe took BMW’s 3.4-liter inline-six, codenamed M30, rebuilt it with forged Mahle pistons, reworked ports, a new camshaft, and lowered its compression ratio before fitting it with two water-cooled Garrett T25 turbochargers.
The main result was almost doubling the M30’s output to no less than 360 PS (355 HP) and a massive 520 Nm (384 lb-ft) of torque. The secondary, but more important result, was a 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) acceleration time of just 5.6 seconds and a top speed reaching 291 kph (181 mph). At the time, this kind of performance, especially for a car with five seats and a large trunk, put the B10 Bi-Turbo in the same performance bracket as a Ferrari Testarossa.
In fact, at launch, the Alpina B10 Bi-Turbo was not only the fastest production sedan on the planet but was also the fastest production car of any type made in Germany. The Porsche 911 Turbo 993 only beat it in 1995, and the sedan record stood until Brabus arrived in 1996 with the E V12, which is obviously also part of the following list. Only 507 B10 Bi-Turbos were built between 1989 and 1995, which surprisingly also made it the best-selling Alpina model in the company’s history until that point.
Porsche 928 GTS: “The Chicken Was Still Warm” As history tells us, the Porsche 928 was initially meant to replace the 911 in the 1970s. Obviously, it never did, albeit it became the purest Autobahn Porsche built up to that time. Launched in 1977, the model was unlike any previous Porsche, since instead of having an air-cooled flat-six in the rear it sported a water-cooled aluminum V8 at the front.
It also had a transaxle layout for its transmission for near-ideal weight distribution, a large trunk with a hatchback, room for four people and an otherworldly high speed stability. The last part was even complemented by Jeremy Clarkson, who has never been a Porsche fan, in a heart-warming story about his ill father.
Photo: Porsche AG The 928’s V8 first offered 240 PS from a displacement of 4.5 liters, but over the next decade or so was constantly refined and improved by Porsche, with the line ending with the 928 GTS. Presented at the end of 1991, the GTS version was the last and most powerful member of the 928 lineage, and it used a 5.4-liter V8 that delivered 350 PS (345 HP) and 500 Nm (369 lb-ft) of torque.
While it was far from beating the Alpina B10 Bi-Turbo in straight-line performance, the 928 GTS was no slouch for what was essentially a comfortable grand tourer. It could go from 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) in 5.7 seconds and had a top speed of 275 kph (171 mph), well over the German 250 kph gentleman agreement, albeit Porsche had never adhered to it anyway.
With that in mind, very few German cars of the era could cover ground as fast and as comfortable as a 928, especially in GTS guise, on a de-restricted part of the Autobahn. This is what made it iconic, and most Porsche fans consider the GTS as the best 928 of them all, a fact seen in used-car prices.
Ruf CTR2: The Air-Cooled 911 That Outgunned the Entire World While most cars on this list were built to cruise the Autobahn with no issues at around or over 250 kph (155 mph), the Ruf CTR2 was built to embarrass almost every production car that tried to follow it on a de-restricted part of the German highway.
Based in Bavaria, Ruf has long been a boutique carmaker that starts with a standard Porsche and then modifies it so much that it needs to stamp its own VIN number on it. It first became world-famous in 1987, when the original CTR “Yellowbird” arrived to completely demolish the Porsche 959 and the Ferrari F40 regarding their top speed.
Photo: Ruf “CTR” originally stood for Group C Turbo Ruf, and it quickly became a legendary moniker. Fast forward into the 1990s, and Alois Ruf, the company’s founder, wanted a “Yellowbird” successor to keep his company at the top of the performance game. That successor came in the form of the CTR2, this time based on the 993-generation 911.
Ruf had deliberately chosen the more narrow body of the 911 Turbo over the wider 911 GT2 for better aerodynamics, and thus, a higher top speed. The CTR2’s engine was an air-cooled, twin-turbocharged flat-six, which was reworked by Ruf engineers to deliver no less than 520 PS (513 HP) and 686 Nm (506 lb-ft) of torque, or about 144 horsepower per liter.
It sent all that oomph through a six-speed manual to either the rear wheels or to all four of them, as customers could choose the car to be AWD. This kind of firepower, combined with a lightweight kevlar body and improved aerodynamics resulted in a top speed of 350 kph (217 mph), making it the fastest production car in the world before it was beaten in 1998 by the McLaren F1. Only 16 of them were built though, with another 16 using the CTR2 Sport moniker, on account of having a 580 PS (572 HP) version of the engine and other modifications.
Brabus E V12 (W210): The Twelve-Cylinder E-Class That Nobody Expected to Destroy the Autobahn While Brabus was already known for transforming seemingly ordinary Mercedes-Benz models into absurdly fast versions. It was the E V12 that transformed that philosophy into a Guinness Book world record. The basic idea had first emerged in 1993, when the Bottrop company decided to squeeze a larger displacement version of the M120 V12 from the S-Class into the engine bay of a W124 E-Class.
After Mercedes-Benz introduced the W120 generation of the E-Class in 1995, Brabus decided to do that feat again, only much bigger. The engine powering the E V12 (W210) was called the Brabus 7.3S, and it was a similar M120 but enlarged to no less than 7,255 cc with bespoke internals. This translated into an output of no less than 582 PS (574 HP) and 772 Nm (569 lb-ft) of torque, sent to the rear wheels through an automatic transmission.
Photo: Brabus The 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) acceleration time for the E V12 was 4.9 seconds, while its top speed was electronically limited to 330 kph (205 mph). According to Brabus, the reason behind the limiter was that no tires available at the time could safely support such a heavy car at a higher speed, albeit the car could do more.
In October 1996, the Guinness Book of Record listed the Brabus E V12 as the world’s fastest street-legal sedan, a title that remained in Bottrop until Brabus beat it again with the W211-based E V12 Biturbo in 2005, which reached over 350 kph (218 mph) at the Nardo test track, in Italy.
What made the original E V12 so legendary was not that it broke that record, but the manner in which it did, as the car was so discreet-looking that it could have easily passed as a German taxi with some aftermarket wheels. In short, it was a regular-looking executive sedan that could outrun most supercars on the Autobahn.
Mercedes-Benz SL 73 AMG: The Secret Roadster That Also Lent Its V12 Heart to a Supercar You’d never guess it just by looking at it, but the last car on this list never set foot in a Mercedes-Benz showroom or on any official price list. In the late 1990s, you simply had to somehow know that it existed, order it with a lot of money, and then just wait. Developed partly in secret, the Mercedes-Benz SL 73 AMG was thought of before the Affalterbach tuner officially became part of the Mercedes family.
It wasn’t the first V12 SL modified by AMG, but it featured the best that the tuner could throw at the venerable roadster, which had already been on sale for a decade. The standard SL’s most powerful factory version was the SL 600, which used the 6.0-liter M120 V12 that powered every big Mercedes of the 1990s. Like Brabus with most of their cars, AMG decided that the SL 600 was not powerful enough, so they bored and stroked the M120 V12 to no less than 7.3 liters and fitted it with forged internals.
Photo: Mercedes-AMG This increased its output to 525 PS (518 HP) and a 750 Nm (553 lb-ft), which was some serious firepower for a naturally aspirated engine back then. This completely transformed the SL from a fast and comfortable cruiser to an Autobahn brute that still wore a tuxedo. Its official top speed was still electronically limited to 250 kph (155 mph), but with the limiter switched off and a mildly different final ratio it could easily go beyond 322 kph (200 mph).
Surprisingly, that isn’t even its single most important claim to fame, as its AMG-tuned engine also made its way under the hood of one of the coolest supercars of the early 2000s. Allegedly around 85 units of the SL 73 were built between 1999 and 2001, when the aging SL was replaced by a new generation. Around the same time, a small supercar manufacturer named Pagani was looking for a more powerful V12 for the latest evolution of the Zonda.
This is how in 2002, when the M120 and all its variants were no longer offered on any Mercedes, the same 7.3-liter V12 from the SL 73 AMG arrived in the Zonda C12 S 7.3. This time, it was tuned to 555 PS (547 HP), and various evolutions of the same V12 went on to power Zondas for the next two decades, which is why the SL 73 AMG is often called the Zonda’s father, not just the last Autobahn monster from the 1990s.

Ridden: Ausom's Dual-Motor GoSoul 2 Surprises With Speed, Comfort, and Acceleration for Low Bucks
46 photos
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution
Until a few years ago, the trusted bicycle was the go-to solution for moving around our towns. But, with the electrification of our world, it’s the e-scooter has grown to be a rival to the bicycle and these days, there are countless brands to choose from. One team’s gear that we’ve been testing is Ausom, and after spending some time on the dual-motor GoSoul 2, I can say that Ausom may have struck an “ausom” balance between cost and capability.
The name Ausom is one that has, in recent years, grown to be known the world over for their budget-oriented e-scooters. With options priced as low as $600 and as high as $1,500, this brand has positioned itself against already established giants in the game and is there swinging swinging.
However, a lower price doesn’t mean less capability, with some Ausom products reaching speeds of over 45 mph. The way they managed to do so is by going with a design that gives us the necessities of speed, comfort, power, and in most cases, off-roading abilities.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution That brings us to their GoSoul 2 with two motors (GoSoul 2 Pro for US), a trinket which I’ve had the pleasure of testing, and one that is now in the hands of my nephew and being ridden alongside the single-motor GoSoul 2 , which, mind you, has now clocked in well over 1,000 miles, with the only servicing needed in that time, being a new set of tires and brake pads. Let’s see how the dual-motor options fares.
Design Evaluation Overall, the dual-motor option isn’t very different from the standard single-motor one, with the same deck design, same folding ability, charge port placement, and for Europe, even similar battery sizes. The suspension is the same, along with cable-driven brakes too. Turn signals are still integrated into the handlebar and head and taillight ensure you’re seen at night and the footboard includes the same lighting.
One difference is found at the cockpit, where the dual-motor option now includes the dual-motor engage button.
Yet, the biggest and most important trait is the presence of that second motor. With it, the GoSoul lineup is taken to the next level, with punchier acceleration and kick, and the ability to keep going in a wider range of scenarios .
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution A big downside of having a second motor, on the other hand, is draining your battery faster.
For US residents, that shouldn’t be a problem as the dual-motor option (Pro) has a larger battery than the standard GoSoul 2, but for Europe, there only a difference of a few tens of Wh between the two models, and this did play an essential role in range tests, especially if you’re slamming the throttle to the max for miles at a time; 645 Wh is all we can play with here.
The rest of the e-scooter is completed with E-ABS at the front and rear, pneumatic tires with tread that I found to offer more grip than on the standard model, and an easy-to-read LCD display. Pretty standard, but all that changes once you hop on this bugger.
A short design evaluation because there isn’t anything new to mention really; it’s the same base the single-motor GoSoul 2 is built upon. Yet, they are two entirely different beasts.
Ride Time Now, it’s in the ride department that the dual-motor option really shines , and I aimed to expose the e-scooter to as many scenarios as possible. In doing so, I found this trinket’s strengths and why Ausom continues to sell their rides.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution First and foremost, the presences of yet another 1,100 W (peak) motor means punchy acceleration, especially in Race mode. Simply put, if you’ve never ridden a dual-motor option, you will have to approach the model starting with lower speed settings and proper body positioning, and this is true for this e-scooter too.
As you accelerate, lean forward a bit so that you’re not thrown backward, and while braking, lean back, so that you don’t pull a scorpion on the road.
On a straightaway, I was consistently reaching 32 kph (20 mph) in as little as 3-4 seconds in Race mode and this acceleration doesn’t ease off until you reach around 50-55 kph; the top speed is 60 kph (37 mph). Forty-eight newton meters (35 lb-ft) of total torque can be produced by these two motors.
Since I’ve tested quite a few Ausom products over the years, the brand gave me the steps to unlocking the e-scooter’s top speed, so my testing was done with this puppy firing on all twos, so to speak.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution I mean, how many of us actually ride e-scooters within limits set by the law? I won’t lie and say that I do; I don’t always. But I do respect road signs, traffic, and ride at low speed if I need to move through pedestrians.
The thing about riding around like a bat out of hell , and with both motors blazing is that range was greatly impacted, and as much as I hate to say it, with a full charge, I was only pulling in around 30-35 km (19-22 mph) with the throttle open as much as possible and still leaving somewhere around 10% of juice in the tank.
This however, is not the sort of experience that I had in a busy urban setting with pedestrians, cars, small obstacles, and the inability to fly around as fast as possible. In such a setting, and with an average speed of around 30 kph (180.6 mph), I was pulling in around 45 km (28 miles), and that’s in a city that does include some hills and the like, not to mention rougher roads in some areas.
Once drained, however, the dual-motor option does take a bit longer to charge, with Ausom mentioning as much as 8.5 hours, but where I was experiencing around 7 hours, and there’s a reason for that: I stayed on top of charging.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution Just like the previous model we tested, the dual-motor GoSoul’s battery gauge in one of the oddest and most questionable around. It’s just very difficult to gauge how much juice you have in the tank since a period of high acceleration can cause the meter to show that you’ve dropped 40% in range, and as you slow down, come back up 20%. Turn the scooter off, and you may see a full gauge once again, only to quickly disappear after riding for a few hundred yards or so.
I understand why it does this, and I’m sure Ausom is aware of the issue – regenerative braking is a major factor - but it would mean coming up with a new set of hardware and software. Maybe the next generation of Ausom products may spit our a better battery gauge and reading.
Hence why I would typically place the unit on charge once I’d see the last bar consistently be the only one visible while riding and stopping. Still, it makes for some, “I need to get home!” moments.
Now, if there’s one thing the GoSoul lineup as a whole does very well, it’s offer a pretty soft ride, especially in an urban setting. This is all down to the adjustable C-arm suspension that we find on this scooter as standard. Not only can we mess around with the level of softness, but this is a tested and proven system for keeping an e-scooter stable, planted, and taking up bumps from the road.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution While flying around on smooth tarmac is clearly on the menu for the system, it’s when you hit a missing patch of tarmac, a crack, or come off a curb that the GoSoul 2 shines. Not only does it reduce just how much of a shock is sent into your body, but it also helps keep those wheels in contact with the ground.
Furthermore, this setup is the same that we find on e-scooters designed for off-road use, and if I may, this model did just fine on hard-pack dirt roads with the occasional sticks and stones.
Hills are also no issue for the dual-motor option, with any one that I can find in my town, being downright demolished by the e-scooter. According to Ausom, up to 27% hill grades are on the menu for this one, but I feel that it reaches a bit higher than that, to as much as 30-35%.
There are hills in my area that showcase this incline, and the Ausom made it up then, albeit, a bit sluggishly toward the top.
Aside from performance , a suspension is also responsible for comfort on an e-scooter, and the C-arm is perfect for that.
It invites you to stay in the saddle for as long as possible, even though the 20-inch deck (length) could use an inch or two more for a slightly wider stance. Luckily we have the footpad at the rear, but that’s more for when you accelerate and not cruising.
Now, just like the standard GoSoul, the dual-motor option is equipped with cable-driven disc brakes, and while my previous review of the single-motor GoSoul did reveal that this lineup falls short in the braking department, for this version, I did see an improvement, resulting in shorter braking distances.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution The single-motor version granted braking distances of around 11 feet at 30 kph (18 mph). As for the dual-motor option, that braking distance is reduced to around 9 ft even though the brakes are essentially the same and the same e-ABS is present.
This means that braking performance comes down to nothing more than tires, and if you compare the two models, you’ll see that the dual-motor option is using a tread that’s more inclined toward off-road use. Kind of counter intuitive, if you ask me, but this is what my tests were yielding.
At higher speeds, like any e-scooter out there, braking distances greatly increase, and fishtailing also comes in to have a say in the matter, so be sure to know how to control speeds like these and don’t actually tap into them if you’re in a crowded setting. Choose your time and place for fun and feeding your adrenaline.
One aspect of the design that I had mixed feelings about is the handlebar, in particular, it’s width. While it helps to keep the scooter stable at speed, it can pose a problem if you need to bob and weave through cars and tight traffic. It’s over 28 inches long, and the placement of the turn signals are responsible for some of that number.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution Clearly, the added weight of another motor and larger battery does make it harder to maneuver this one around town with the folding frame and locking mechanism at the rear. On days where I didn’t eat breakfast, I could really feel the extra 6 lbs or so of added weight as opposed to the single-motor option.
With the initial generation, I had a bit of an issue with the latch that hold the deck and steering column united for transport, and for this version, the same system is used. It can slip on you if not properly secured, so be careful with that one.
Riding at night with the GoSoul 2 also felt reasonably safe and controllable. Not only do the headlight and taillight signal to other road goers of your presence, but the integrated lighting does the same, casting an easy-to-see blue glow around the deck.
The turn signals, on the other hand, are a bit questionably placed. If you’re wearing a jacket, cars and vehicles behind you won’t easily see your intention as the elbow typically covers and visibility from the rear. From the front, it’s fine.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution The usual NFC card can be used with the display, along with a code, and while I personally enjoy the layout and its visibility, I did notice that with polarized sunglasses, it’s a bit difficult to see, disappearing almost entirely from view until you shift your head a bit. Toss in a weight limit of 130 kg (287 lbs), and we have ourselves a dual-motor GoSoul 2.
Why a Dual-Motor E-Scooter One benefit of a dual-motor e-scooter that is not to be overlooked, and a reason why I would recommend starting off with one anyway, even if it is your first e-scooter, is just that: there are two motors.
Not only does this grant us access to speed and acceleration, but if you’re not ready for the second motor just yet, use only one; you’ll quickly outgrow it, especially if you do a bit of reading on proper riding technique and the like.
Basically, you’d be buying an e-scooter that you can grow with, and frankly, 60 kph (37 mph) is plenty of speed in an urban setting; gear up properly out there.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution Furthermore, no one says you have to ever use the second motor, and in a setting where you’re trying to squeeze out as much range as possible out of your battery, the ability to ride around with just one active is not to be overlooked.
Price All this is going to run you as little as €600 ($650), if you grab one now, as part of a Black Friday sale and “AusomBF” discount code. Normally, the dual-motor option, for Europeans, as least, costs €700.
For the US, however, the dual-motor GoSoul carries the Pro tag, and does come with some extra goodies, including a larger battery and stronger motors. It’s selling for $850 as part of the Black Friday sale. Otherwise, it costs $1,000.
Conclusion Sure, the dual-motor GoSoul 2 isn’t perfect, but then again, what is? Sure, some downsides in the form of the questionable battery gauge, speed that calls for hydraulic brakes, and that folding latch that can slip are there, but the benefits greatly outweigh the rewards.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin for Autoevolution The two motors means “ausom” acceleration, no more than we can handle or need, the same is true for top speed, and the suspension that Ausom chose to build the model around does it’s job like a charm.
Sure, it has limits, like any system, but for cities with rough roads, and even the occasional hard-pack dirt road, the C-arm setup is great. Don’t forget that you can adjust the springs too.
Simply put, it’s a good deal; go for it.
